analysis.one_liner: Tightens wage, recruitment, and anti-outsourcing rules on employers of H-1B visa workers.
analysis.headline: A bill raising H-1B worker protections was introduced by one representative with five cosponsors in 2005 and never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have raised the wage floor for H-1B guest workers by requiring employers to pay the highest of several wage benchmarks, forced employers to prove they recruited and did not displace U.S. workers for 180 days, banned staffing firms from farming H-1B workers out to other companies, cut the visa's duration from six years to three, removed an exemption from visa caps for foreign master's degree holders, tripled the employer petition fee, and let workers sue employers who violated the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. tech and professional workers, who would face stronger rules against being displaced or undercut by lower-paid H-1B labor, and H-1B workers themselves, who would gain a higher wage floor, earlier notice of applications, and a private right to sue over violations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: U.S. tech workers and H-1B employees

how_it_helps.text: Employers would have to pay H-1B workers the greatest of three wage measures — the local prevailing wage, the median wage for the occupation in the area, or the median for skill level two in the government's wage survey — instead of being able to pick a lower benchmark [S2] [S3].

The window during which employers must show they did not displace a U.S. worker would double from 90 to 180 days, and the requirement would extend to all H-1B employers, not just H-1B-dependent ones [S2] [S3].
Employers would be barred from outsourcing, leasing, or contracting H-1B workers out to other companies, a rule aimed at staffing and body-shop firms [S2] [S3].
Workers harmed by a violation of these labor conditions could sue the employer directly in court for damages [S2] [S3].

The Labor Department would be made responsible for investigating wage complaints and application fraud, could audit all H-1B employers annually, and must audit employers whose H-1B workforce is 15% or more of their staff [S2] [S3].
The visa cap exemption for foreigners holding a U.S. master's degree or higher would be eliminated, and the maximum stay cut from six years to three, tightening the overall supply [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers of H-1B workers — particularly IT staffing and outsourcing firms and large tech companies — would pay higher wages, a tripled $4,500 petition fee, audit exposure, litigation risk, and a shorter, tighter visa program.

drawbacks.text: The bill cuts the maximum H-1B stay from six years to three and eliminates the master's-degree cap exemption, which would sharply reduce the program's usefulness for employers and could push skilled work offshore rather than raise wages [S2] [S3].

Tripling the petition fee to $4,500 and requiring W-2 disclosure would add significant compliance cost to every H-1B filing, costs that small employers and universities would bear along with large firms [S2] [S3].

A broad private right of action would open employers to civil lawsuits for any violation of the labor condition rules, which critics of such provisions typically argue invites litigation even over paperwork errors [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real wage and displacement protections for U.S. and foreign workers, but its blunt tools — halving the visa term, removing the master's exemption, and tripling fees — would also shrink legal skilled immigration substantially, raising the honest objection that it curbs the program rather than fixing it.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Judiciary Committee, then in its immigration subcommittee, and died there when the 109th Congress ended without any hearing or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Pascrell of New Jersey introduced the bill on November 17, 2005, joined by Reps. Owens, Waters, and Kilpatrick [S1] [S3].
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day [S5].
On February 6, 2006, it was referred to the subcommittee on Immigration, Border Security, and Claims, and no further action was taken before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5].
The bill never received a committee vote, a floor vote, or a companion Senate introduction [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: H-1B employers — especially IT staffing and outsourcing firms — avoided higher wage floors, a tripled fee, audit exposure, and lawsuit risk; no worker received the bill's protections.

for.name: Rep. Bill Pascrell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to tighten H-1B wage, recruitment, and enforcement rules.

for.name: Reps. Owens, Waters, and Kilpatrick
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction [S3]; additional cosponsors later brought the total to five [S4].

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after its November 2005 referral, never scheduled a hearing or markup.

against.name: Subcommittee on Immigration, Border Security, and Claims
against.what_they_did: Received the referral in February 2006 and took no action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican supported the bill in the record, and the Republican-majority committee never acted on it [S1] [S4].

industries.note: These firms place H-1B workers at client companies, a business model the bill's outplacement ban would prohibit outright, and they face the highest audit and lawsuit exposure. Their gain from the bill's death was the survival of that model.
Large tech companies would pay the tripled $4,500 fee, higher wage floors, and a shorter three-year visa term. Killing the bill preserved their lower-cost, longer-duration access to foreign labor.
Removing the cap exemption for U.S. master's-degree holders would reduce a path universities use to place foreign graduates in jobs. The bill also subjects degree requirements to tighter scrutiny.

They would gain a higher wage floor, 30-day advance notice, and a right to sue, but lose the six-year stay and the master's-degree cap exemption. The bill's title and text frame them as beneficiaries alongside domestic workers.
